questions.title: health
questions.passage: Many teenagers treat sleep as something they can sacrifice whenever life gets busy. Yet a growing number of researchers argue that enough sleep is absolutely crucial for teenagers, not a luxury to be traded for an extra hour of studying. During the teenage years, the brain is still developing, and sleep is when it stores memories and repairs itself. When students are constantly short of rest, the overall result appears quickly, because concentration weakens and mood becomes unstable. Some experts even warn that a chronic lack of sleep may harm long-term health. Critics may respond that ambitious students simply have too much to do. However, this argument confuses being busy with being effective. Doctors generally recommend that teenagers sleep at least eight hours each night, and schools that start later often report calmer classrooms. The lesson is clear: protecting sleep is not laziness but a sensible choice that helps a young mind learn faster.

Busy students always perform better.

questions.title: science
questions.passage: Bees are small insects, but they do a very important job for nature. When a bee lands on a flower, it looks for sweet food called nectar. While the bee drinks, tiny yellow grains called pollen stick to its body. Then the bee flies to another flower and leaves some of that pollen there. This simple act helps the plant make seeds and grow new fruit. Without it, many flowers could not spread or produce the food we eat. Apples, melons, and many vegetables need bees in this way. Because bees move from flower to flower all day, they help whole fields of plants stay healthy. Sadly, the number of bees is falling in many places today. If we protect bees, we also protect the plants and food that people and animals need.

questions.title: community
questions.passage: Last weekend, more than forty students from Greenvale Senior High School gathered at the banks of the Maple River to take part in a clean-up day called "Clear Waters." The event was organized by the school's Eco Action Club, which wanted to protect the river that runs through their town. Volunteers arrived early on Saturday morning, wearing gloves and carrying large bags. They spent four hours collecting plastic bottles, broken toys, and other rubbish that had washed up along the shore. According to club leader Mia Chen, the team removed enough waste to fill a small truck. Local residents were surprised by how much had been hidden among the reeds. Several parents joined in, and a nearby cafe offered free drinks to everyone who helped. The students hope to hold a similar event every season so the river stays clean. Many volunteers agreed that the experience made them feel more connected to their community.
